name: NewDeductions
plan: Plan 1: married equal earners at $300,000 each file separate returns in both years and each deducts State and local tax under the word-for-word reading of 26 U.S.C. 164(b)(6)-(7) (reduce the applicable limitation amount, floor it at $10,000, then halve): $13,075 each for 2026, against $11,900 for the couple on a joint return

tests.detail: The grammar supports only reduce-floor-halve and the plan survives the strict re-run, but the reading is a hand-set flag, the default branch is mislabelled as the IRS worksheet, and $1,050 of the gain comes from giving all household payments to one spouse.
With the reduction applied to the halved amount the plan falls to $1,052 (plan 3, not SALT) and the baseline does not move.
Each of the six moves is needed for the full figure and removing all unused moves leaves it unchanged; the plan is one one-year plan run twice.
Under the pre-2025 $10,000/$5,000 cap separate returns save $210 (2026 charity floor), and nothing once the 2026 charity and section 68 changes are also removed.
No conservation or absurd-goal violation in any reachable position of 18 runs over 10 households plus a zero-income household; checks not mutation-tested.

Kernel replays of plan, baseline and closed-gap result, and a theorem over all move sequences that the closed-gap rule never reaches the plan's figure; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
Python written from the statute text gives the same baseline, plan tax and gain to the dollar.
Nothing closes the plan; the IRS 2025 Schedule A worksheet itself uses reduce-floor-halve, contradicting the Findings, and the JCT explanation could not be retrieved.

divergences: saltLiteral is an author-set switch and positions 7L/7bL exist only for this plan; the search did not find the reading

the default branch (20,200 less 30%, floor 5,000) is labelled the IRS worksheet but is not; it matches no ordering of the statute's words and understates every separate return over $252,500 in the other positions (plan 2: 7,464 printed, 7,866 on the worksheet computation)
all property tax, instalment, mortgage interest and gifts are given to spouse A; split equally the gain is 9,974 (the other 1,050 is plan 3)
no AMT in the model (checked outside it: none due)
year 2 uses 2026 dollar amounts instead of the 101% amounts for 2027
separate-filer losses not modelled: section 21 dependent care credit, State return status, filing cost; IRA, education and student-loan items are already phased out at this income
gain exists only for MAGI of about $252,500 to $353,833 each (equal earners) with State and local tax above the limit on each return

authority.source: IRS, Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040) (2025), State and Local Tax Deduction Worksheet, line 5e
authority.quote: Yes. Enter $40,000 ... 5. Enter $500,000 ($250,000 if married filing separately) ... 7. Multiply line 6 by 30% (0.30) 8. Subtract line 7 from line 1 9. Enter the larger of the amount on line 8 or $10,000 10. State and local tax deduction. Enter the smaller of the amount on line 9 (half the amount on line 9 if married filing separately) or the amount from Schedule A, line 5d

authority.source: IRS Publication 17 (2025), What's New and chapter 11
authority.quote: The overall limit is reduced if your modified adjusted gross income is more than $500,000 ($250,000 if married filing separately) but will not be reduced below $10,000 ($5,000 if married filing separately). For more information, see the Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040).

authority.source: fedratecalc.com SALT deduction calculator (rules checked October 28, 2026; read through a summarising fetch)
authority.quote: the full amount becomes $40,000 − $15,000 = $25,000, and the cap is half of that, $12,500

authority.source: Joint Committee on Taxation, General Explanation (JCS-1-26)

verdict_reason: The statute's words allow only reduce, floor, then halve; the figure reproduces in the kernel and in independent arithmetic, vanishes under the closing edit and under earlier law, and the IRS 2025 worksheet computes it the same way. The Findings are wrong that the IRS halves first, the reading was supplied by a flag and not found by the search, and the SALT gain alone is $9,974 over two years, not $11,024.
